I am fifty years old, and I have been farming this land in Quzhou since I was a young girl. I never went to school, so I cannot read the words on fertilizer bags, but I know the soil here on the North China Plain by touch and by season. The wheat I sowed last October is sleeping under the soil, and now it is nearly Qingming — the green-up time. I will walk my fields every morning to see if the wheat has broken dormancy evenly. 

My family has six mu of good flat land. I do not gamble with strange crops. Every household in my village grows winter wheat followed by summer maize; this is the iron law of the double-cropping calendar. If I planted something different and the market price collapsed, my family would have no grain and no cash. So this year, just like last year and my mother’s years before me, I will put all six mu into the wheat–maize rotation. 

For the wheat that is already in the ground, I will spread a topdressing of urea when the tillers show, because the village supply store told me this “improved” wheat seed — the kind with the short stiff stalk — is hungry for nitrogen at green-up. I will irrigate three times: once now to wake the wheat, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once at grain-filling so the kernels plump. I never skip irrigation; the sky here does not give enough rain in spring. I will also spray pesticide three times — the first with herbicide to kill the winter weeds, then insecticide when the aphids come, and once more if I see rust spots on the leaves. Before sowing the wheat last autumn I rotary-tilled the maize stubble into the soil, so that work is already done. I expect about 1,000 jin of wheat per mu if the late spring does not turn dry and hot.

As soon as the wheat is harvested in early June — and I mean the very same week, because the summer season does not wait — I will plant hybrid maize. Everyone uses no-tillage now for the maize; we cut the wheat straw low and sow the maize seeds directly into the stubble with a machine. It saves time and fuel, and the leftover straw keeps some moisture in the July heat. I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing, then irrigate twice: once right after planting to help germination, and once at the big trumpet-leaf stage when the cobs are forming. Three pesticide sprays should be enough — herbicide first, then insecticide for the corn borer, and maybe fungicide if the summer is very wet. Hybrid maize usually gives me a bit more than wheat; I hope for 1,100 jin per mu.

I have thought about growing vegetables or cotton like some neighbors, but my husband and I are getting older, and our children work in the city. Wheat and maize are the only crops we can manage with our own hands and one small tractor. They are safe. The state buys wheat at a guaranteed price, and there is always a market for maize. That is enough for us.
